title: The Himalayas: Roof of the World
summary: The Himalayas are the tallest mountain range on Earth, formed by colliding tectonic plates and home to Mount Everest.
poll: Mountains that are still growing are more interesting than mountains that stay the same.

versions.title: The Himalayas: Roof of the World
versions.text:
The Himalayas are tall mountains. They sit high up. People call them the Roof of the World. They have the tallest peaks on Earth.

Long ago, two big plates met. They pushed hard. The land rose up. It made big mountains. The plates still push. The range still grows.

The range is long. It crosses five lands in Asia.

Mount Everest is the tallest peak. It stands here. Many want to climb it. The air up high is thin. It is hard to breathe.

Sherpas live close by. They help climbers. Yaks are big and strong. They carry loads. Snow leopards hunt in the snow.

Ice called glaciers sits high up. It melts bit by bit. It makes rivers below. The rivers give water to many.

The Earth is warm now. The ice melts fast. This worries people. The range will always amaze us.

versions.title: The Himalayas: Roof of the World
versions.text:
Seen from far away, the Himalayas may look like one solid wall of rock and snow. Up close, however, each peak holds its own story. The Himalayas are not simple hills. They were not always this tall. They are made of layers pushed up from deep inside the Earth!

Each layer of rock began far below the surface. To build the range, huge plates pushed hard against each other. Old rock bent and cracked under the pressure. New pressure then pushed it even higher. Thousands of these layers stacked up over millions of years. Slowly, the folded rock rose into one giant range.

High on the slopes, thick glaciers slowly creep downhill. They grind against rock as they move. They carve out deep, steep valleys over time. In return, melting glaciers feed the rivers that start high in these mountains.

The range is a busy home for Sherpas, yaks, snow leopards, and many other living things. They find shelter in its deep valleys. They find food and water there too.

The Himalayas hold some of the tallest peaks on Earth. Many of the highest sit along the border between Nepal and China. The air up high is cold and holds little oxygen. Scientists have found that climbers react very differently to such thin, high air.

Even so, climbing here is full of danger. Sometimes the air holds too little oxygen for too long. Then climbers can grow weak, dizzy, and confused. This is called altitude sickness. Storms and falling ice can also badly hurt climbers.

People are working to make climbing safer. Climbers should follow trained Sherpa guides. Expeditions should carry proper gear and oxygen tanks. Everyone can respect this huge, fragile mountain range. Together, we can protect the Himalayas.

versions.title: The Himalayas: Roof of the World
versions.text:
Seen from a distance, the Himalayas may look like a single wall of rock and snow. Up close, however, the range is bursting with geologic history. The Himalayas are not just old hills. They are one of the youngest great mountain ranges on Earth.

Deep below the surface, two huge plates of the Earth's crust collided long ago. The collision did not stop after one push. As the plates kept moving, the land between them kept folding. Over tens of millions of years, these folds piled up and formed a massive range.

High on the slopes, thick glaciers slowly creep downhill under their own weight. The moving ice grinds against rock below it, and it carves deep, steep valleys as it goes. In return, this melting ice feeds the rivers that begin high in these mountains.

The Himalayas cover only a small part of Asia's land, but they hold more of the world's highest peaks than any other range. Sherpas, yaks, and snow leopards all shelter in the range's deep valleys. The mountains also shape the region's weather, blocking cold winds and holding back rain clouds.

Mount Everest, the tallest peak on Earth, sits at the heart of this great range, and it has drawn climbers from every country. The air near its summit holds barely a third of the oxygen found at sea level. Scientists have studied how little oxygen the human body can handle that high up.

Even so, climbing here is full of danger. When climbers spend too long at extreme altitude, their bodies grow weak, dizzy, and confused. This is called altitude sickness. Storms, falling ice, and avalanches can also badly hurt climbers near the summit.

People are working to make expeditions safer. Climbing teams now carry proper gear and oxygen tanks. Trained Sherpa guides lead most expeditions up the mountain. Everyone can help by respecting this huge, fragile mountain range.

versions.title: The Himalayas: Roof of the World
versions.text:
Seen from a distance, the Himalayas may resemble a single, continuous wall of rock and snow, but beneath that surface the range reveals one of the most dramatic geologic histories on the planet. The Himalayas are not ancient, worn-down hills; rather, they are among the youngest great mountain systems on Earth, and they continue to rise today.

Deep below the surface, two enormous tectonic plates collided long ago in a process geologists call continental collision, and that collision has never fully stopped. As the plates continued pushing against each other, the land caught between them kept folding, buckling, and rising. Over tens of millions of years, these folds piled up and formed the massive mountain system we recognize today, while erosion from wind, rain, and ice slowly wore away at the rising peaks, even as the range's elevation kept increasing.

Behind the range lies the Tibetan Plateau, a vast, high, flat expanse that is itself one of the highest regions on Earth. High on the Himalayan slopes, thick glaciers creep slowly downhill, grinding against rock and carving deep valleys as they melt into the rivers below.

The Himalayas cover only a small part of Asia's land, yet they hold more of the world's highest peaks than any other mountain system. Sherpas, yaks, and snow leopards all shelter in the range's deep valleys, while the mountains themselves shape the region's weather, blocking cold winds and holding back the rain clouds that feed the summer monsoon.

Mount Everest, the tallest peak on Earth, rises at the heart of this great range alongside other giants such as Kangchenjunga and Lhotse, and it draws costly, carefully planned expeditions from every corner of the world each year. The air near its summit holds barely a third of the oxygen found at sea level, placing the human body under extreme stress.

This extreme altitude makes climbing extraordinarily dangerous. When climbers spend too long at such heights, their bodies grow weak, dizzy, and confused, a condition known as altitude sickness. Storms, falling ice, and sudden avalanches add further danger near the summit.

People are working to make expeditions safer. Climbing teams now carry proper gear and oxygen tanks, and trained Sherpa guides lead most expeditions up the mountain. Everyone can help by respecting this immense, fragile mountain system.

versions.title: The Himalayas: Roof of the World
versions.text:
The Himalayas constitute a colossal, snow-covered mountain system that arcs across the roof of Asia for roughly 2,400 kilometers, separating the Indian subcontinent from the vast, arid Tibetan Plateau to the north and effectively dividing two of the most populous regions on Earth. For centuries, inhabitants of the region have referred to this range as the Roof of the World, and the designation fits remarkably well, since the Himalayas contain a far greater share of Earth's loftiest peaks than any other mountain system on the planet.

Tens of millions of years ago, the Himalayas did not exist in any recognizable form. Two enormous tectonic plates, drifting slowly across the globe for tens of millions of years, eventually collided head-on with tremendous and unrelenting force, in a process geologists call continental collision, since neither plate was dense enough to slide beneath the other. The land caught between the two plates had nowhere to go but upward, so it folded, buckled, and was thrust into towering peaks that are, remarkably, still forming today at a measurable rate. Because the plates continue to push together, the Himalayas are still gaining elevation by a few millimeters each year, a surprisingly substantial amount of uplift across geological time, though erosion from wind, rain, and glacial ice wears the peaks down simultaneously, carving the dramatic, steep-sided valleys that define the landscape.

Just behind the range sits the Tibetan Plateau, a vast, high, flat expanse that is itself one of the highest and driest regions on Earth, sometimes nicknamed the Third Pole because it stores so much of the world's ice outside the polar regions. The range itself passes through five countries and regions: Nepal, India, Pakistan, Bhutan, and China, each of which governs and protects its own share of these peaks.

Mount Everest, the tallest peak on the planet, rises nearly nine kilometers above sea level at the heart of this great range, alongside other giants such as Kangchenjunga and Lhotse. Thousands of climbers from every corner of the world join costly, meticulously planned expeditions each year, hoping to reach Everest's icy summit before the brief weather window closes. Near the top, the altitude is so extreme that the air holds barely a third of the oxygen found at sea level, so most climbers must carry oxygen tanks simply to keep breathing in what guides often refer to as the death zone, where the human body slowly deteriorates the longer it remains.

Sherpa families have inhabited villages near the mountains for countless generations, and their deep, practical knowledge of the terrain has made them indispensable guides on difficult, costly, and occasionally fatal expeditions. Sturdy yaks haul heavy loads up narrow paths, while rare, well-camouflaged snow leopards hunt quietly among the high, rocky snow.

Thick glaciers blanket many of the highest slopes, storing frozen water that accumulated gradually over thousands of years. Slowly, this ancient ice melts into rushing streams that flow downhill and feed some of Asia's largest rivers, including the Ganges, the Indus, and the Brahmaputra, carrying fresh water to hundreds of millions of people living far below in the plains.

Today a warming climate is causing many Himalayan glaciers to melt faster than ever recorded, and scientists worry this could seriously disrupt the rivers that so many communities depend on for drinking water, farming, and electricity. Even so, the great Himalayas continue to fill travelers and scientists alike with awe, drawing new expeditions and new research every single year.

LOW.prompt: What are the Himalayas, and why are they an amazing place? Use details from the article.

LOW.modelAnswer: The Himalayas are a huge mountain range in Asia, formed when two big plates of rock pushed into each other and folded the land upward. They are amazing because they hold the tallest peak on Earth, Mount Everest, and because thick glaciers on their slopes melt into rivers that give water to many people. Snow leopards and yaks live high in these mountains, and Sherpa people help climbers on hard trips up Everest.

MID.prompt: Explain how the Himalayas formed and why melting glaciers matter for people far from the mountains. Use evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained how the Himalayas formed.
I described why melting glaciers matter.
I used evidence from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: The Himalayas formed when two huge tectonic plates collided and pushed the land between them upward into towering peaks, a process that still continues today. This matters for people far from the mountains because thick glaciers store ice that slowly melts into rivers like the Ganges, the Indus, and the Brahmaputra, giving fresh water to hundreds of millions of people. Because a warming climate is making these glaciers melt faster than before, scientists worry that the water supply for drinking and farming could change, which shows how a faraway mountain range can still affect people's daily lives.

HIGH.prompt: Explain the tectonic process that created the Himalayas and why their glaciers matter far beyond the mountains themselves. Use evidence about elevation, erosion, and the rivers described in the article.
checklist: I explained the tectonic process that formed the Himalayas.
I connected the mountains' glaciers to people living far away.
I supported my ideas with evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: The Himalayas formed through continental collision, a tectonic process in which two enormous plates drifted toward each other for tens of millions of years before colliding with such force that the land between them folded and was thrust upward into towering peaks. Because the plates continue pushing together, the range keeps gaining elevation even today, although erosion from wind, rain, and glacial ice wears the peaks down at the same time. These glaciers matter far beyond the mountains themselves because their slow melt feeds major rivers such as the Ganges, the Indus, and the Brahmaputra, which hundreds of millions of people depend on for drinking water, farming, and electricity. Since a warming climate is accelerating this melt, the fate of a distant mountain range is now tied directly to the daily lives of people living across an entire region.
